claim: Class-B1 G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are an important family of clinically relevant drug targets that remain difficult to investigate via high-throughput screening and in animal models.
source: Class-B1 G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are an important family of clinically relevant drug targets that remain difficult to investigate via high-throughput screening and in animal models.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance and challenges of studying class-B1 GPCRs, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: PAClight1P78A is a novel genetically encoded sensor based on the human PAC1 receptor (hmPAC1R).
source: Here, we engineered PAClight1P78A, a novel genetically encoded sensor based on a class-B1 GPCR (the human PAC1 receptor, hmPAC1R)
evidence: The manuscript describes the engineering of this sensor as a primary finding of the work.

claim: PAClight1P78A has a high dynamic range of ΔF/F0 = 1100%.
source: Here, we engineered PAClight1P78A, a novel genetically encoded sensor based on a class-B1 GPCR (the human PAC1 receptor, hmPAC1R) endowed with high dynamic range (ΔF/F0 = 1100%)
evidence: The dynamic range value is explicitly stated and supported by experimental measurements shown in the manuscript.

claim: PAClight1P78A has excellent ligand selectivity.
source: Here, we engineered PAClight1P78A, a novel genetically encoded sensor based on a class-B1 GPCR (the human PAC1 receptor, hmPAC1R) endowed with high dynamic range (ΔF/F0 = 1100%), excellent ligand selectivity
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates through specificity screening that the sensor responds to PACAP but not to VIP or other peptides.

claim: PAClight1P78A has rapid activation kinetics with τON = 1.15 s.
source: Here, we engineered PAClight1P78A, a novel genetically encoded sensor based on a class-B1 GPCR (the human PAC1 receptor, hmPAC1R) endowed with high dynamic range (ΔF/F0 = 1100%), excellent ligand selectivity, and rapid activation kinetics (τON = 1.15 s).
evidence: The activation time constant is explicitly stated and supported by kinetic measurements shown in Figure 1f.

claim: PAClight1P78A shows robust expression and fluorescence responses upon exogenous ligand application ex vivo in mice.
source: Demonstrating its use in animal models, we show robust expression and fluorescence responses upon exogenous ligand application ex vivo and in vivo in mice
evidence: The manuscript presents data from acute brain slice experiments showing sensor responses to PACAP application.

claim: PAClight1P78A shows robust expression and fluorescence responses upon exogenous ligand application in vivo in mice.
source: Demonstrating its use in animal models, we show robust expression and fluorescence responses upon exogenous ligand application ex vivo and in vivo in mice
evidence: The manuscript presents fiber photometry data from behaving mice showing sensor responses to PACAP microinjections.

claim: PAClight1P78A shows robust expression and fluorescence responses in living zebrafish larvae.
source: Demonstrating its use in animal models, we show robust expression and fluorescence responses upon exogenous ligand application ex vivo and in vivo in mice, as well as in living zebrafish larvae.
evidence: The manuscript presents two-photon imaging data from zebrafish larvae showing sensor responses to PACAP injection.

claim: Class-B1 GPCRs are the focus of intense and rapidly expanding drug development efforts.
source: Class-B1 G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) represent an important sub-group of peptide-sensing GPCRs, that are the focus of intense and rapidly expanding drug development efforts (Hauser et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Peptide agonists have been extremely successful in the clinical treatment of type-2 diabetes and obesity.
source: Class-B1 G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) represent an important sub-group of peptide-sensing GPCRs, that are the focus of intense and rapidly expanding drug development efforts (Hauser et al., 2017), driven by extremely successful examples of peptide agonists used in the clinical treatment of metabolic human diseases, such as type-2 diabetes and obesity (Wang et al., 2022b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PACAP is an endogenous 38-amino acid peptide.
source: PACAP is an endogenous 38-amino acid peptide that is among the most phylogenetically conserved peptides (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about PACAP structure, supported by citation.

claim: PACAP is among the most phylogenetically conserved peptides.
source: PACAP is an endogenous 38-amino acid peptide that is among the most phylogenetically conserved peptides (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PACAP1-27 has 68% homology with vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
source: Its shorter C-terminally truncated form (i.e., PACAP1-27) has 68% homology with the vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) (Dickson and Finlayson, 2009).
evidence: This statement about sequence homology is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors can both be equipotently activated by VIP and PACAP.
source: In fact, VIP and PACAP share a subfamily of class-B1 GPCRs, of which the two receptors VPAC1 and VPAC2 can both be equipotently activated by VIP and PACAP (Dickson and Finlayson, 2009).
evidence: This statement about receptor pharmacology is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PAC1 receptor has a reported affinity for PACAP that is 100- to 1000-fold higher than its affinity to VIP.
source: The third receptor in this subfamily, that is the PAC1 receptor (PAC1R, also known as ADCYAP1R1), however, has a reported affinity for PACAP that is 100- to 1000-fold higher than its affinity to VIP (Dickson and Finlayson, 2009).
evidence: This statement about receptor affinity is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PACAP and its receptors are found throughout the central and peripheral nervous system, the immune system, in endocrine glands as well as in other organ systems and in many cancerous tissues.
source: The tissue distribution of PACAP and its receptors is widespread and they can be found throughout the central and peripheral nervous system, the immune system, in endocrine glands as well as in other organ systems and in many cancerous tissues (Dickson and Finlayson, 2009; Hashimoto et al., 1996; Condro et al., 2016; PACAP, 2016; Blechman and Levkowitz, 2013).
evidence: This statement about tissue distribution is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The PACAP/PAC1R system has been linked to protective functions in the nervous and immune systems.
source: A large body of evidence has linked the PACAP/PAC1R system to protective functions in the nervous and immune systems, as well as to stress- and anxiety-related behaviors (in particular post-traumatic stress disorder), migraine, nociception, thermoregulation, sleep/wake cycles, and reproductive functions (Dickson and Finlayson, 2009; PACAP, 2016; Biran et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The PACAP/PAC1R system has been linked to stress- and anxiety-related behaviors, particularly post-traumatic stress disorder.
source: A large body of evidence has linked the PACAP/PAC1R system to protective functions in the nervous and immune systems, as well as to stress- and anxiety-related behaviors (in particular post-traumatic stress disorder), migraine, nociception, thermoregulation, sleep/wake cycles, and reproductive functions (Dickson and Finlayson, 2009; PACAP, 2016; Biran et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The PACAP/PAC1R system has been linked to migraine, nociception, thermoregulation, sleep/wake cycles, and reproductive functions.
source: A large body of evidence has linked the PACAP/PAC1R system to protective functions in the nervous and immune systems, as well as to stress- and anxiety-related behaviors (in particular post-traumatic stress disorder), migraine, nociception, thermoregulation, sleep/wake cycles, and reproductive functions (Dickson and Finlayson, 2009; PACAP, 2016; Biran et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Genetically encoded GPCR-based sensors enable the direct optical detection of GPCR activation by agonist ligands with high sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution.
source: Recently, genetically encoded GPCR-based sensors have been developed that enable the direct optical detection of GPCR activation by agonist ligands with high sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution (Patriarchi et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2020; Patriarchi et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2020; Oe et al., 2020; Duffet et al., 2022; Duffet et al., 2023; Kagiampaki et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature describing GPCR-based sensors.

claim: Only a few GPCR-based sensors are built from class-B1 peptide-sensing GPCRs.
source: While these tools hold great potential for drug development, pharmacology, and neuroscience applications, only a few of them are built from class-B1 peptide-sensing GPCRs (Duffet et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The initial sensor prototype PAClight0.1 showed clear intracellular retention.
source: This initial prototype construct, named PAClight0.1, was expressed on the surface of HEK293T cells, but showed clear intracellular retention and a very weak average fluorescent response to bath application of PACAP1-38 (ΔF/F0 = 43.4%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This observation is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: PAClight0.1 showed a very weak average fluorescent response to bath application of PACAP1-38 (ΔF/F0 = 43.4%).
source: This initial prototype construct, named PAClight0.1, was expressed on the surface of HEK293T cells, but showed clear intracellular retention and a very weak average fluorescent response to bath application of PACAP1-38 (ΔF/F0 = 43.4%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Reintroduction of Q336 before the cpGFP module improved the average fluorescent response to PACAP1-38 (ΔF/F0 = 343%).
source: This led us to the identification of a second mutant, in which Q336 was reintroduced before the cpGFP module, that showed improved average fluorescent response to the ligand (ΔF/F0 = 343%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Mutation of residue T468 to alanine improved the overall surface expression of the sensor in HEK293T cells.
source: Mutation into alanine of residue T468, a reported post-translational modification site (https://www.phosphosite.org) on the C-terminus of the receptor (Hornbeck et al., 2004), improved the overall surface expression of the sensor in HEK293T cells and further increased the observed average fluorescent response (ΔF/F0 = 516%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–g).
evidence: This observation is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The T468A mutation further increased the observed average fluorescent response to ΔF/F0 = 516%.
source: Mutation into alanine of residue T468, a reported post-translational modification site (https://www.phosphosite.org) on the C-terminus of the receptor (Hornbeck et al., 2004), improved the overall surface expression of the sensor in HEK293T cells and further increased the observed average fluorescent response (ΔF/F0 = 516%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–g).
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: T468 is a reported post-translational modification site on the C-terminus of the PAC1 receptor.
source: Mutation into alanine of residue T468, a reported post-translational modification site (https://www.phosphosite.org) on the C-terminus of the receptor (Hornbeck et al., 2004)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a database and previous literature.

claim: The ICL2 mutant F259K/F260K/P261K displayed a largely improved fluorescent response to PACAP1-38 (ΔF/F0 = 942%).
source: Our functional screen of a library of ICL2 mutants led to the identification of one variant comprising three point mutations (F259K/F260K/P261K) that displayed a largely improved fluorescent response to PACAP1-38 (ΔF/F0 = 942%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–g).
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: PAClight1 has excellent surface expression and fluorescent response (ΔF/F0 = 1037%).
source: Upon introduction of the C-term T468A mutation on the ICL2 F259K/F260K/P261K background, we obtained an improved version of the sensor, named PAClight1, with excellent surface expression and fluorescent response (ΔF/F0 = 1037%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Application of a high concentration of VIP onto PAClight1-expressing cells caused a large fluorescent response corresponding to more than half of the response to PACAP1-38 (ΔF/F0 = 654%).
source: Indeed, application of a high concentration of VIP onto sensor-expressing cells caused a large fluorescent response, corresponding to more than half of the response to PACAP1-38 (ΔF/F0 = 654%, Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The P78A mutation abolished the sensor response to VIP while leaving unaltered the response to PACAP1-38.
source: Through this screening, we identified a single mutation (P78A) that abolished the sensor response to VIP while leaving unaltered the response to PACAP1-38 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c, d).
evidence: This observation is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: PAClight1P78A reaches a mean ΔF/F0 of 1066% in HEK293T cells upon bath application of 10 μM PACAP1-38.
source: Upon bath application of 10 μM PACAP1-38, PAClight1P78A reaches a mean ΔF/F0 of 1066% in HEK293T cells (n = 3, five regions of interest [ROIs])
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: PAClight1P78A reaches a mean ΔF/F0 of 883% in rat primary neurons upon bath application of 10 μM PACAP1-38.
source: Upon bath application of 10 μM PACAP1-38, PAClight1P78A reaches a mean ΔF/F0 of 1066% in HEK293T cells (n = 3, five regions of interest [ROIs]) and a mean ΔF/F0 of 883% in rat primary neurons (n = 3, five ROIs).
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The excitation maximum of PAClight1P78A in the saturated state is at 498 nm.
source: The excitation maximum of the saturated state is at 498 nm.
evidence: This measurement is supported by spectral characterization data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The isosbestic point of PAClight1P78A is at 420 nm.
source: The isosbestic point is at 420 nm.
evidence: This measurement is supported by spectral characterization data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The emission maximum of PAClight1P78A in the saturated state is at 514 nm.
source: Emission maximum in of the saturated state is at 514 nm.
evidence: This measurement is supported by spectral characterization data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The activation time constant of PAClight1P78A upon application of PACAP1-38 is τON = 1.15 s.
source: The trace shown is the average of three independent experiments.
evidence: This measurement is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 1f, which shows the activation time constant.

claim: The kinetics of class-B1 GPCR sensors can be used to infer the occupancy of the ECD by an antagonist peptide.
source: Our previous work on the development of another class-B1 sensor based on the GLP1 receptor, led us to discover that the kinetics of the sensor's response can be used to infer the occupancy of the ECD by an antagonist peptide (Duffet et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The PAClight1P78A response was approximately fourfold slower in the presence of the extracellular antagonist PACAP6-38.
source: The PAClight1P78A response was strikingly slower (approximately fourfold) in the presence of the extracellular antagonist, and was in the range of 1 s in its absence (Figure 1f, g).
evidence: This observation is supported by kinetic measurements shown in Figure 1f and 1g.

claim: After bath application of 200 nM PACAP1-38, there was no decrease in PAClight1P78A signal nor any internalization observed over 100 frames.
source: After bath application of 200 nM PACAP1-38 (slow diffusion of the peptide with 10× dilution from 2 μM to 200 nM) there was no decrease in signal, nor any internalization observed.
evidence: This observation is supported by long-term imaging data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Max.d.4 can outcompete PACAP1-38 at PAClight1P78A, albeit not to a full extent under the specified experimental conditions.
source: Within 45–50 frames after application of the PAC1R antagonist, the signal intensity steadily decreased and started to plateau slightly above baseline levels. This indicates, that Max.d.4 can outcompete PACAP1-38 at PACligth1P78A, albeit not to a full extent under the specified experimental conditions.
evidence: This observation is supported by long-term imaging data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Mammalian PACAP1-38 displayed the strongest potency in PAClight1P78A activation (1052% ΔF/F0).
source: Mammalian PACAP1-38 displayed the strongest potency in PAClight1P78A activation (1052% ΔF/F0, t(3) = 40.31, 95% CI [9.69, 11.35], p < 0.001).
evidence: This measurement is supported by specificity screening data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Chicken PACAP1-38 (chPACAP38) activated the PAClight1P78A sensor with strong but slightly reduced potency (896% ΔF/F0).
source: Both of these homologs of the mammalian PACAP1-38 activated the PAClight1P78A sensor with strong but slightly reduced potency (chPACAP38: 896% ΔF/F0, t(4) = 11.17, 95% CI [6.73, 11.19], p = 0.0066
evidence: This measurement is supported by specificity screening data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Zebrafish PACAP21-27 (zfPACAP2) activated the PAClight1P78A sensor with strong but slightly reduced potency (898% ΔF/F0).
source: Both of these homologs of the mammalian PACAP1-38 activated the PAClight1P78A sensor with strong but slightly reduced potency (chPACAP38: 896% ΔF/F0, t(4) = 11.17, 95% CI [6.73, 11.19], p = 0.0066; zfPACAP2: 898% ΔF/F0, t(3) = 11.49, 95% CI [6.46, 11.41], p = 0.024).
evidence: This measurement is supported by specificity screening data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Maxadilan activated PAClight1P78A with lower potency than mammalian PACAP1-38 (416% ΔF/F0).
source: Consistent with the reported activity of Maxadilan on the hmPAC1Rnull receptor, we detected activation of PAClight1P78A by Maxadilan, however, with lower potency than mammalian PACAP1-38 (416% ΔF/F0, t(3) = 9.47, 95% CI [2.76, 5.56], p = 0.04).
evidence: This measurement is supported by specificity screening data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Maxadilan was previously identified to be a specific ligand of the PAC1R but not to the VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors.
source: Furthermore, we also screened the sand fly salivary gland-derived peptide Maxadilan, which was previously identified to be a specific ligand of the PAC1R but not to the VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors (Lerner et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The Drosophila gene amn (amnesiac) is homologous to the mammalian gene encoding PACAP (Adcyap1).
source: The Drosophila gene amn (amnesiac) was previously shown to be homologous to the mammalian gene encoding PACAP (Adcyap1) and amn Drosophila mutants show memory impairments similar to rodent PACAP/PAC1R mutants (Feany and Quinn, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The insect peptide encoded by amn did not significantly activate PAClight1P78A above baseline (26% ΔF/F0).
source: We therefore also tested whether this insect peptide encoded by amn would activate PAClight1P78A, but no significant activation above baseline was observed (26% ΔF/F0, t(2) = 3.2, 95% CI [−0.09, 0.61], p = 0.69).
evidence: This measurement is supported by specificity screening data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The response of PAClight1P78A to VIP was not significantly above baseline (57% ΔF/F0).
source: Therefore, the response of PAClight1P78A to VIP in this specificity screen was also not significantly above baseline (57% ΔF/F0, t(2) = 11.09, 95% CI [0.35, 0.79], p = 0.12).
evidence: This measurement is supported by specificity screening data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: None of the tested class-B1 GPCR ligands (CRF, PTH, GLP-1) or class-A GPCR ligands (OXY, OXA-OXB, MCH, DYN, ENK, N-OFQ, NPFF, NPS, NT, NB) activated the PAClight1P78A sensor above baseline level.
source: Other peptides tested in this screen included other class-B1 GPCR ligands (corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF), parathyroid hormone (PTH), and glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1)), as well as some peptidergic class-A GPCR ligands (oxytocin (OXY), orexin-A and -B (OXA–OXB), melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH), dynorphin (DYN), enkephalin (ENK), nociception (N-OFQ), neuropeptide FF (NPFF), neuropeptide S (NPS), neurotensin (NT), and neuromedin B (NB)). None of these neuropeptides activated the PAClight1P78A sensor above baseline level (Figure 2b).
evidence: This observation is supported by specificity screening data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: PAClight1P78A does not recruit miniGs upon stimulation with PACAP1-38.
source: Yet, we did not detect recruitment of either miniGs, miniGsq, or β-arrestin2 in PAClight1P78A-expressing cells upon stimulation with PACAP1-38.
evidence: This observation is supported by NanoLuciferase complementation assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PAClight1P78A does not recruit miniGsq upon stimulation with PACAP1-38.
source: Yet, we did not detect recruitment of either miniGs, miniGsq, or β-arrestin2 in PAClight1P78A-expressing cells upon stimulation with PACAP1-38.
evidence: This observation is supported by NanoLuciferase complementation assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PAClight1P78A does not recruit β-arrestin2 upon stimulation with PACAP1-38.
source: Yet, we did not detect recruitment of either miniGs, miniGsq, or β-arrestin2 in PAClight1P78A-expressing cells upon stimulation with PACAP1-38.
evidence: This observation is supported by NanoLuciferase complementation assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wild-type PAC1R recruits miniGs, miniGsq, and β-arrestin2 upon activation with 1 μM of PACAP1-38.
source: As expected, we observed significant miniGs, miniGsq, and β-arrestin2 recruitment to the wild-type PAC1R upon activation with 1 μM of PACAP1-38.
evidence: This observation is supported by NanoLuciferase complementation assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The carboxylic group of D3 in PACAP is crucial for binding affinity and biological activity to all three receptor types (PAC1, VPAC1, and VPAC2).
source: The carboxylic group of D3 was shown to be crucial for binding affinity and biological activity of PACAP to all three receptor types (i.e., PAC1, VPAC1, and VPAC2) (Doan et al., 2011; Bourgault et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Residues Y161 and R199 of the hmPAC1R interact with residue D3 of PACAP.
source: Furthermore, the cryo-EM structure of the hmPAC1R in interaction with PACAP identified residues Y161 and R199 of the hmPAC1R to interact with residue D3 of PACAP (Kobayashi et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a cryo-EM structure study.

claim: Residue Y161 forms a hydrogen bond with D3 of PACAP.
source: Residue Y161 forms a hydrogen bond with D3, while R199 forms an electrostatic interaction with D3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This statement is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Residue R199 forms an electrostatic interaction with D3 of PACAP.
source: Residue Y161 forms a hydrogen bond with D3, while R199 forms an electrostatic interaction with D3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This statement is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The R199A mutation on PAClight1 drastically reduced the average fluorescent response to 41.9% ΔF/F0.
source: This single-point mutant showed drastically reduced average fluorescent response (PAClight1: 1075% ΔF/F0, PAClight1_R199A: 41.9% ΔF/F0, Figure 2—figure supplement 2c) to 10 μM PACAP1-38.
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: The double mutant PAClight1-ctrl (R199A/Y161A) completely reduced the fluorescent response to PACAP1-38 to baseline levels (2.87% ΔF/F0).
source: To further abolish the remaining response, we additionally mutated Y161 into alanine (Y161A) on the previous backbone (i.e., PAClight1_R199A_Y161A) and named the construct 'PAClight1-ctrl'. This completely reduced the fluorescent response to PACAP1-38 to baseline levels (PAClight1-ctrl: 2.87% ΔF/F0).
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: PAClight1P78A-ctrl showed an abolished fluorescent response to PACAP1-38 (10.44% ΔF/F0) in transfected HEK293T cells.
source: Next, we cloned these two point mutations into the backbone of PAClight1P78A and observed an equally abolished fluorescent response to PACAP1-38 (PAClight1P78A: 1034% ΔF/F0, PAClight1P78A-ctrl: 10.44% ΔF/F0, t(4.03) = 37.89, p < 0.0001, 95% CI [1098.63, 949.02], two-sided two-sample Welch's t test, Figure 2—figure supplement 2d) in transfected HEK293T cells
evidence: This measurement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2d.

claim: PAClight1 has 2.15-fold higher basal brightness than dLight1.3b.
source: Statistical comparison of the distributions of the two cell lines shows 2.15-fold higher basal brightness of PAClight1 over dLight1.3b (t(4.74) = 19.254, p < 0.0001, 95% CI [−1.30,−0.99], two-sided two-sample Welch's t test, Figure 2d).
evidence: This measurement is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2c and 2d.

claim: The median of the standard deviation in the FITC-A channel across the titration series was 62.6% smaller in the stable PAClight1P78A relative to the transfected PAClight1P78A condition.
source: The median of the standard deviation in the FITC-A channel across the titration series was 62.6% smaller in the stable PAClight1P78A relative to the transfected PAClight1P78A condition (p = 0.0142, Figure 3b).
evidence: This measurement is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: PAClight1P78A has a slightly lower affinity (EC50 = 29.91 nM) than PAClight1 (EC50 = 22.97 nM) toward PACAP1-38.
source: The titration dataset reveals a slightly lower affinity of the PAClight1P78A sensor (EC50 = 29.91 nM) than the PAClight1 sensor (EC50 = 22.97 nM) toward PACAP1-38 (Figure 3d).
evidence: This measurement is supported by dose-response curve data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The affinity of the PAClight1 sensor toward VIP (EC50 = 1.238 μM) is much lower than its affinity toward PACAP1-38.
source: The affinity of the PAClight1 sensor (non-specific mutant) toward VIP (EC50 = 1.238 μM) is much lower than its affinity toward PACAP1-38 (Figure 3d).
evidence: This measurement is supported by dose-response curve data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The 100-1000× difference in affinity between VIP and PACAP1-38 on PAClight1 is well in accordance with previous reports on the differential affinities of VIP and PACAP1-38 on the PAC1R.
source: This 100–1000× difference is well in accordance with previous reports on the differential affinities of VIP and PACAP1-38 on the PAC1R (Cauvin et al., 1990; Buscail et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: No response of PAClight1P78A to the addition of VIP up to a concentration of 50 μM was detected.
source: We were not able to detect any response of PAClight1P78A to the addition of VIP up to a concentration of 50 μM (linear regression p = 0.079, Figure 3d)
evidence: This observation is supported by dose-response curve data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Publicly available RNAseq databases show strong expression of PACAP receptor (Adcyap1r1) in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus of mice and humans.
source: Publicly available RNAseq databases (in situ hybridization atlas from the Allen Institute: https://alleninstitute.org/) and previous work (Zhang et al., 2021) show strong expression of PACAP receptor (Adcyap1r1) in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus of mice and humans
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to public databases and a citation to previous literature.

claim: PAClight1P78A fluorescence increased by +6.8% ΔF/F0 when bath applying 300 nM of PACAP1-38 in acute brain slices.
source: PAClight1P78A fluorescence increased by +6.8 and +17.5% ΔF/F0 when bath applying 300 and 3000 nM of PACAP1-38, respectively (Figure 4d).
evidence: This measurement is supported by acute brain slice imaging data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: PAClight1P78A fluorescence increased by +17.5% ΔF/F0 when bath applying 3000 nM of PACAP1-38 in acute brain slices.
source: PAClight1P78A fluorescence increased by +6.8 and +17.5% ΔF/F0 when bath applying 300 and 3000 nM of PACAP1-38, respectively (Figure 4d).
evidence: This measurement is supported by acute brain slice imaging data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Comparing PAClight1P78A fluorescence with PAClight1P78A-ctrl fluorescence revealed a statistically significant difference when bath applying 3000 nM of PACAP1-38 in acute brain slices.
source: Comparing PAClight1P78A fluorescence with PAClight1P78A-ctrl fluorescence revealed a statistically significant difference when bath applying 3000 nM of PACAP1-38 (Figure 4d).
evidence: This statistical comparison is supported by acute brain slice imaging data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: PAClight1P78A clearly increased its fluorescence in response to 3 µM PACAP1-38 (+17.5% peak ΔF/F0) but not to VIP (−5.5% peak ΔF/F0), CRF (−4.3% peak ΔF/F0), or ENK (+1.4% peak ΔF/F0) in acute brain slices.
source: PAClight1P78A clearly increased its fluorescence in response to 3 µM PACAP1-38 (+17.5% peak ΔF/F0), but not to VIP (−5.5% peak ΔF/F0), CRF (−4.3% peak ΔF/F0), or ENK (+1.4% peak ΔF/F0) (Figure 4e).
evidence: This measurement is supported by acute brain slice imaging data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: In acute mouse brain slices, PAClight1P78A detects concentrations of >300 nM of PACAP1-38 in superfused bath application.
source: In conclusion, our data show that in acute mouse brain slices, PAClight1P78A detects concentrations of >300 nM of PACAP1-38 in superfused bath application, while not reacting to other neuropeptides tested.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the dose-response and specificity data from acute brain slices.

claim: Microinfusion of PACAP1-38 (300 µM, 200 nl) led to peak fluorescence increases of 165.5 ± 58.0% ΔF/F0 in PAClight1P78A-expressing mice.
source: Microinfusion of PACAP1-38 (300 µM, 200 nl) led to peak fluorescence increases of 165.5 ± 58.0% ΔF/F0 in PAClight1P78A-expressing mice.
evidence: This measurement is supported by in vivo fiber photometry data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The fluorescence peaked at 28 min after PACAP1-38 microinfusion in PAClight1P78A-expressing mice.
source: The fluorescence peaked at 28 min and dropped to 128.6 ± 45.7% ΔF/F0 1 hr after, when injections were positioned in average 318 µm from the recording site.
evidence: This measurement is supported by in vivo fiber photometry data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: PAClight1P78A-ctrl-expressing mice showed a fluorescence increase of only 16.7 ± 2.6% ΔF/F0 after PACAP1-38 microinfusion.
source: In contrast, PAClight1P78A-ctrl-expressing mice showed a fluorescence increase of only 16.7 ± 2.6% ΔF/F0 (Figure 4g).
evidence: This measurement is supported by in vivo fiber photometry data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: PACAP1-38 diffuses efficiently across hundreds of µm in neocortical brain areas of mice.
source: Moreover, our data suggest that PACAP1-38 diffuses efficiently across hundreds of µm, with slow extracellular degradation in neocortical brain areas of mice.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the in vivo fiber photometry data showing responses at distances of ~318 µm from the injection site.

claim: PACAP1-38 has slow extracellular degradation in neocortical brain areas of mice.
source: Moreover, our data suggest that PACAP1-38 diffuses efficiently across hundreds of µm, with slow extracellular degradation in neocortical brain areas of mice.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the sustained fluorescence response observed in the in vivo experiments.

claim: Zebrafish larvae are an important animal model that has long been recognized for its utility and applicability to drug discovery.
source: Zebrafish larvae are an important animal model that has long been recognized for its utility and applicability to drug discovery (MacRae and Peterson, 2015; Zon and Peterson, 2005; Sturtzel et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: PAC1 signaling has been associated with the adaptive stress response of zebrafish.
source: Moreover, PAC1 signaling has been associated with the adaptive stress response of zebrafish (Biran et al., 2020; Amir-Zilberstein et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Based on a publicly available scRNAseq dataset, the olfactory region of 4-day post-fertilization (dpf) old zebrafish larvae expresses high levels of Adcyap1b in ~75% of cells composing the olfactory region.
source: Based on a publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) dataset (Farrell et al., 2018), we identified the olfactory region of 4-day post-fertilization (dpf) old zebrafish larvae to express high levels of Adcyap1b in ~75% of cells composing the olfactory region.
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis of a publicly available dataset cited in the text.

claim: A strong increase in PAClight1P78A fluorescence was observed already at ~120 s post-ICV injection with ΔF/F0 levels continuously rising until the end of the post-ICV injection recordings in zebrafish.
source: We observed a strong increase in PAClight1P78A fluorescence already at ~120 s post-ICV injection with ΔF/F0 levels continuously rising until the end of the post-ICV injection recordings (Figure 5d, d'').
evidence: This observation is supported by two-photon imaging data from zebrafish shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Peak ΔF/F0 levels and the area under the curve significantly differed between PACAP1-38/saline and saline-only injected zebrafish animals.
source: Peak ΔF/F0 levels and the area under the curve significantly differed between PACAP1-38/saline and saline-only injected animals (nsaline = 5, nPACAP1-38 = 5, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test p = 0.0079, Figure 5e, e').
evidence: This statistical comparison is supported by two-photon imaging data from zebrafish shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The condition median for peak ΔF/F0 levels was 70-fold larger in PACAP1-38/saline injected zebrafish animals (145.76% ΔF/F0) than in saline-only injected animals (2.06% ΔF/F0).
source: The condition median for peak ΔF/F0 levels was 70-fold larger in PACAP1-38/saline injected animals (145.76% ΔF/F0) than in saline-only injected animals (2.06% ΔF/F0) (Figure 5e).
evidence: This measurement is supported by two-photon imaging data from zebrafish shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Considerable variability in the extent of the dynamic range was observed between different regions of interest (ROIs) within the same and also between different zebrafishes.
source: However, we noticed considerable variability in the extent of the dynamic range displayed by different regions of interest (ROIs) within the same and also between different zebrafishes (Figure 5d'', e').
evidence: This observation is supported by two-photon imaging data from zebrafish shown in Figure 5d'' and 5e'.

claim: PAClight1P78A combines a very large dynamic range with excellent PACAP selectivity and good membrane expression.
source: The final sensor construct, named PAClight1P78A (Figure 1a, b, Supplementary file 1), includes all the above-mentioned mutations and combines a very large dynamic range with excellent PACAP selectivity and good membrane expression, and was thus selected for further in vitro characterization.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the characterization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Future work could explore whether a grafting-based approach could lead to the direct generation of multiple class-B1 sensors based on the optimized fluorescent protein module from PAClight.
source: Given the very high sensitivity of these tools, future work could explore whether a grafting-based approach, similar to the one we recently described for class-A GPCR-based sensors (Kagiampaki et al., 2023), could lead to the direct generation of multiple class-B1 sensors based on the optimized fluorescent protein module from PAClight.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications of the sensor.

claim: PAClight1P78A is intended to be employed when there is an experimental need to ensure maximal selectivity of the response for the endogenous ligand PACAP1-38.
source: Given the higher PACAP selectivity of PAClight1P78A, this sensor variant is intended to be employed when there is an experimental need to ensure maximal selectivity of the response for the endogenous ligand PACAP1-38 (e.g., if the sensor is to be used for attempting the detection of endogenous PACAP1-38 release).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the characterization of the sensor's selectivity.

claim: For all experimental scenarios other than detecting endogenous PACAP release, PAClight1 can be a better choice as it retains the original wild-type sequence in its ECD.
source: For all other experimental scenarios, PAClight1 can be a better choice, as it retains the original wild-type sequence in its ECD and thus most closely represents the natural ligand-binding profile of the human PAC1 receptor.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the characterization of the sensor variants.

claim: Variations in diffusion rates and spatial diffusion patterns of PACAP1-38 within the brain parenchyma and cortical tissue may contribute to inter- and intraindividual differences in maximal sensor response.
source: An intriguing alternative explanation, supported by the observation of continuously increasing ΔF/F0 levels (at least within the first 15 min), is that variations in diffusion rates and spatial diffusion patterns of PACAP1-38 within the brain parenchyma and cortical tissue may contribute to these differences.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed variability in sensor responses.

claim: The distance between PAClight1P78A-expressing cells and the site of injection might influence the extent of fluorescent response.
source: Furthermore, the distance between PAClight1P78A -expressing cells and the site of injection might influence the extent of fluorescent response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed variability in sensor responses.

claim: PAClight1/PAClight1P78A-expressing zebrafishes and mice could potentially be used to investigate and validate diffusion properties of PAC1R ligands in live organisms.
source: Under more controlled experimental conditions, PAClight1/PAClight1P78A -expressing zebrafishes and mice could therefore potentially be used to investigate and validate diffusion properties of PAC1R ligands in live organisms at a relatively high throughput or to screen for novel small-molecule or peptide PAC1R agonists and antagonists with improved penetration properties across the ventricular wall.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications of the sensor.

claim: The delayed decay of PAClight1P78A fluorescence may result from the slow clearance of peptides from extracellular space, putatively due to saturation of the enzymatic degradation system.
source: We hypothesize that this delayed decay may result from the slow clearance of peptides from extracellular space, putatively due to saturation of the enzymatic degradation system.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed slow decay of the sensor signal.

claim: An alternative explanation for the delayed decay could be a long-lasting activation of PAC1 after binding of PACAP1-38.
source: An alternative explanation could be a long-lasting activation of PAC1 after binding of PACAP1-38. This explanation is substantiated by slow decay in our slice experiments and by previous findings that PACAP1-38 effects on downstream PKA signaling is longer lasting than effects of two other tested peptides (VIP and CRH) (Hu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis supported by the experimental observations and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The work did not demonstrate the use of PAClight sensors for the detection of endogenous PACAP release in tissues or animal models.
source: Notably, in this work, we did not demonstrate the use of any of our PAClight sensors for the detection of endogenous PACAP release in tissues or animal models, as our focus was deliberately set on the characterization and validation of the tools for applications to drug screening and/or development across species.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about what was not demonstrated in the study.

claim: Based on observations from mouse slice and in vivo recordings, bulk or epifluorescent imaging is unlikely to reveal endogenous release of PACAP.
source: Based on our observations from mouse slice and in vivo recordings, bulk or epifluorescent imaging is unlikely to reveal endogenous release of PACAP, given that measured peptide concentrations typically occur in the femtomolar to nanomolar range (Palkovits et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and a citation about typical PACAP concentrations.

claim: Further optimization of the sensor to increase sensitivity and brightness coupled with the use of two-photon imaging holds promise for future application of this sensor for in vivo detection of endogenously released PACAP.
source: However, further optimization of the sensor to increase sensitivity and brightness coupled with the use of two-photon imaging that allows to focus on PAClight-expressing cell membranes nearby PACAP release sites, holds promise for future application of this sensor for in vivo detection of endogenously released PACAP.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future improvements and applications.

claim: It will be essential to record PACAP release close to the main sites of action to capture physiologically relevant temporal dynamics, considering the slow diffusion of PACAP1-38 observed in in vivo experiments.
source: Considering the slow diffusion of PACAP1-38 observed in our in vivo experiments, it will be quintessential to record PACAP release close to the main sites of action to capture physiologically relevant temporal dynamics.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental observations of slow PACAP diffusion.

claim: The new tools can be valuable assets to investigate real-time dynamics of PAC1 receptor activation in response to the application of specific PAC1 receptor agents, both at a cellular level and in vivo in zebrafish and in the mammalian brain.
source: Our results show that the new tools introduced in this study can be valuable assets to investigate real-time dynamics of PAC1 receptor activation in response to the application of specific PAC1 receptor agents, both at a cellular level and in vivo in zebrafish and in the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The in vivo validation of the sensor demonstrates its ability to reveal diffusion dynamics of applied drugs and peptides within brain tissue.
source: The in vivo validation of our sensor demonstrates its ability to reveal diffusion dynamics of applied drugs and peptides within brain tissue.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the in vivo fiber photometry experiments in mice.

claim: This tool can be employed in applications such as studying the diffusion of novel PAC1-targeting drugs and peptides, thereby offering mechanistic insights into the localization of drug actions in the brain.
source: We therefore suggest that this tool can be employed in applications such as studying the diffusion of novel PAC1-targeting drugs and peptides, thereby offering mechanistic insights into the localization of drug actions in the brain.
evidence: This is a suggested application based on the demonstrated capabilities of the sensor.
